## Cloud Security Posture Management

**Parent L1**: Cloud and Infrastructure Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) is the enterprise capability that continuously assesses the configuration of cloud accounts, services, and resources against established security baselines and compliance frameworks. It provides automated detection of configuration drift from secure baselines, policy-as-code enforcement through AWS Config rules and Service Control Policies, and a unified cross-account posture view through AWS Security Hub. CSPM is the foundational visibility layer across all other Cloud and Infrastructure Security capabilities — a misconfigured IAM role, unencrypted S3 bucket, or publicly exposed security group will surface as a CSPM finding regardless of which operational team is responsible.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Identify (ID.AM — Asset Management; ID.RA — Risk Assessment) and CSF Protect (PR.IP — Information Protection); addresses the need to know, at all times, whether the cloud environment configuration conforms to the security baseline.
**Regulatory Relevance**: CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark, HIPAA Security Rule §164.312(a)(1), NIST 800-53 CM-2 (Baseline Configuration), CM-6 (Configuration Settings), CM-7 (Least Functionality)
**Key Stakeholders**: Security architecture, cloud platform engineering, security operations, compliance
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-CLOUD-CSPM-2.6.03](GUID-SEC-CLOUD-CSPM-2.6.03.md)
**Capability Boundary**: CSPM assesses and alerts on configuration state; it does not govern the runtime behavior of workloads (Workload Protection) or manage the lifecycle of secrets (Secrets Management). CSPM findings for IAM misconfigurations are surfaced here but remediated through Cloud IAM governance processes.

## Workload Protection

**Parent L1**: Cloud and Infrastructure Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: Workload Protection provides runtime threat detection and behavioral monitoring for cloud workloads — EC2 instances, ECS and EKS containers, and Lambda functions. It detects threats that preventive controls did not prevent: anomalous process execution, unauthorized outbound network communication to known-malicious destinations, credential access attempts, lateral movement from a compromised workload, and container escape attempts. Workload Protection is the last-resort detective control layer at the infrastructure level — it assumes that perimeter controls, IAM governance, and vulnerability management have not fully prevented a threat actor from gaining workload access, and it detects that access in near-real time.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Detect (DE.CM — Security Continuous Monitoring; DE.AE — Adverse Event Analysis) and CSF Respond (RS.AN — Incident Analysis); addresses the need to detect exploitation of residual vulnerabilities and misconfigurations before they escalate to data exfiltration or lateral movement.
**Regulatory Relevance**: HIPAA Security Rule §164.312(b) (Audit Controls), NIST 800-53 SI-3 (Malicious Code Protection), SI-4 (System Monitoring)
**Key Stakeholders**: Security operations, cloud platform engineering, incident response team
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-CLOUD-WORKLOAD-PROT-2.6.04](GUID-SEC-CLOUD-WORKLOAD-PROT-2.6.04.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Workload Protection governs cloud-native runtime threat detection; it interfaces with the Endpoint Security domain for EDR tooling governance on EC2 instances. Application-layer detection (WAF, RASP) is Application Security domain responsibility. Network-layer anomaly detection (VPC flow log analysis) is Network Security domain responsibility.

## Secrets Management

**Parent L1**: Cloud and Infrastructure Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: Secrets Management provides lifecycle governance for all infrastructure secrets consumed by cloud workloads and platform services: credentials (database passwords, service account tokens), API keys, TLS certificates, and encryption key material. It establishes centralized secret creation, access control policy, automated rotation, and comprehensive audit logging for all secrets. The capability eliminates the chronic security risk created by hardcoded credentials, manually rotated passwords, and secrets stored in uncontrolled locations such as source code, configuration files, and unencrypted parameter stores. Every secret consumed by a cloud workload has a defined owner, access policy, rotation schedule, and audit trail.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect (PR.AC — Identity Management, Authentication, and Access Control; PR.DS — Data Security for secrets at rest and in transit); addresses the root cause of a large proportion of cloud breach incidents — compromised or exposed credentials.
**Regulatory Relevance**: HIPAA Security Rule §164.312(d) (Person or Entity Authentication), NIST 800-53 IA-5 (Authenticator Management), SC-12 (Cryptographic Key Establishment and Management)
**Key Stakeholders**: Cloud platform engineering, application development teams, security architecture, DevOps
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-CLOUD-SECRETS-MGMT-2.6.05](GUID-SEC-CLOUD-SECRETS-MGMT-2.6.05.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Secrets Management governs infrastructure secrets consumed at the platform and workload layer. Application-level secrets embedded in application configuration are a shared responsibility between this capability (governance policy and tooling) and Application Security (secure coding standards and source code scanning). PKI and certificate authority governance is Identity Security domain responsibility.

## Cloud Identity and Access Management

**Parent L1**: Cloud and Infrastructure Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: Cloud Identity and Access Management governs the design, assignment, and continuous right-sizing of cloud platform identities — IAM roles for workloads and services, EC2 instance profiles, ECS task roles, Lambda execution roles, and Service Control Policies that define the permission boundaries for entire AWS accounts. This capability is distinct from enterprise human identity management (Identity Security domain): it governs what cloud services and workloads are permitted to do, not who human users are or how they authenticate. Least-privilege governance is the central architectural concern: every cloud identity has access only to the specific AWS services and resources required for its documented function, and that access is continuously validated against actual usage patterns.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect (PR.AC — Identity Management, Authentication, and Access Control); cloud IAM misconfiguration — over-privileged roles, missing permission boundaries, absent SCPs — is one of the highest-frequency root causes of cloud security incidents.
**Regulatory Relevance**: HIPAA Security Rule §164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), NIST 800-53 AC-2 (Account Management), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), AC-6 (Least Privilege)
**Key Stakeholders**: Cloud platform engineering, security architecture, application teams
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-CLOUD-CLOUD-IAM-2.6.06](GUID-SEC-CLOUD-CLOUD-IAM-2.6.06.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Cloud IAM governs AWS service and workload identities. Human user access to AWS accounts (federated SSO, MFA enforcement) is Identity Security domain responsibility. Application-level authorization (who can perform what operations within an application) is Application Security domain responsibility.

## Cloud Data Protection

**Parent L1**: Cloud and Infrastructure Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: Cloud Data Protection provides encryption-at-rest governance for cloud-managed storage services — S3, RDS, Aurora, EBS, DynamoDB, EFS, and other storage services hosting Gainwell data. It governs customer-managed key (CMK) usage for workloads handling PHI and other sensitive regulated data, defines KMS key rotation policy, and enforces object storage access controls (S3 bucket policies, public access block enforcement, object ownership). This capability ensures that data-at-rest encryption is not an optional or late-stage addition to cloud workload design — it is a deployment prerequisite enforced at the infrastructure configuration level.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect (PR.DS — Data Security); addresses the obligation to protect PHI at rest under HIPAA and to prevent unauthorized access to regulated data through uncontrolled storage configurations.
**Regulatory Relevance**: HIPAA Security Rule §164.312(a)(2)(iv) (Encryption and Decryption), §164.312(e)(2)(ii) (Encryption), NIST 800-53 SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest), SC-12 (Cryptographic Key Management)
**Key Stakeholders**: Security architecture, cloud platform engineering, data platform teams, compliance
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-CLOUD-DATA-PROT-2.6.07](GUID-SEC-CLOUD-DATA-PROT-2.6.07.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Cloud Data Protection governs data-at-rest encryption and storage configuration at the infrastructure layer. Data classification and data governance policy are Information Security / Data Architecture domain responsibilities. Application-layer encryption (field-level encryption, database column encryption) is outside this capability's scope. Transit encryption is Network Security domain responsibility.

## Cloud Network Security Governance

**Parent L1**: Cloud and Infrastructure Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: Cloud Network Security Governance provides policy compliance enforcement for cloud network configuration — the infrastructure-layer complement to the Network Security domain's architectural design authority. Where the Network Security domain establishes *how* cloud networks should be architecturally designed (VPC segmentation, transit gateway topology, WAF placement), this capability verifies that deployed configurations conform to those design standards and the security baseline. It governs security group rule compliance (no overly permissive inbound rules), private endpoint adoption (no public internet paths for supported services), and VPC configuration assessment (flow logging enabled, default VPC governance). Findings surface through CSPM tooling and trigger remediation workflows.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect (PR.AC — Access Control at network layer; PR.PT — Protective Technology); enforces that cloud network configuration does not create unauthorized access paths to workloads and data.
**Regulatory Relevance**: HIPAA Security Rule §164.312(e)(1) (Transmission Security), NIST 800-53 SC-7 (Boundary Protection), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement)
**Key Stakeholders**: Cloud platform engineering, network engineering, security architecture
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-CLOUD-NETWORK-SEC-2.6.08](GUID-SEC-CLOUD-NETWORK-SEC-2.6.08.md)
**Capability Boundary**: This capability governs *compliance enforcement* for existing cloud network configurations — it does not own cloud network architecture design. VPC architecture, transit gateway design, and Zero Trust network access architecture are Network Security domain responsibilities ([GUID-SEC-NETWORK-CLOUD-NET-2.2.11](../Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-CLOUD-NET-2.2.11.md)). This capability ensures what gets deployed matches what was architected.

## Vulnerability Management

**Parent L1**: Cloud and Infrastructure Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: Vulnerability Management provides systematic identification, prioritization, and remediation tracking for infrastructure-layer vulnerabilities in cloud workloads. It covers OS-level CVEs on EC2 instances and ECS host nodes, container image vulnerabilities in ECS and EKS workloads, and package-level vulnerabilities in Lambda function deployment packages. Vulnerability findings are prioritized by CVSS score with SLA-tiered remediation targets (Critical: 7 days, High: 30 days, Medium: 90 days). Unpatched findings that exceed SLA thresholds trigger pipeline deployment controls that prevent new deployments of affected workload versions until remediation is confirmed. This capability supersedes the patching strategy approach documented in GUID-SEC-CLOUD-PATCHING-STRATEGY-3.6.01 (superseded), which is replaced by the normative requirements in [GUID-SEC-CLOUD-VULN-MGMT-2.6.09](GUID-SEC-CLOUD-VULN-MGMT-2.6.09.md).
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Identify (ID.RA — Risk Assessment) and CSF Protect (PR.IP — Information Protection Processes and Procedures); addresses the accumulation of exploitable vulnerabilities that creates a growing attack surface over time.
**Regulatory Relevance**: HIPAA Security Rule §164.308(a)(5)(ii)(B) (Protection from Malicious Software), NIST 800-53 RA-5 (Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning), SI-2 (Flaw Remediation)
**Key Stakeholders**: Cloud platform engineering, application development teams, security operations, DevOps
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-CLOUD-VULN-MGMT-2.6.09](GUID-SEC-CLOUD-VULN-MGMT-2.6.09.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Vulnerability Management governs infrastructure-layer CVEs in cloud workloads. Application-layer vulnerabilities (SAST findings, SCA for application dependencies, DAST findings) are Application Security domain responsibilities. The SLA and pipeline enforcement mechanisms for both domains should be aligned, but are separately governed.

## Inbound File Scanning

**Parent L1**: Cloud and Infrastructure Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: Inbound File Scanning provides the enterprise capability to intercept, inspect, and disposition all file streams entering Platform Gainwell storage volumes and data systems at the ingest boundary. Every inbound file — regardless of source channel, file type, or submitting identity — is held in a transient staging zone and subjected to malware and virus signature analysis before any promotion to a destination store. Files confirmed clean proceed to their destination. Files detected as infected are quarantined in an isolated store inaccessible to downstream systems, and the Security Operations Center is alerted in real time via a structured event notification. The capability enforces a fail-closed posture: if the scan engine is unavailable or returns an error, file promotion is denied. Scan engine virus definitions are refreshed automatically on a daily minimum cadence to maintain currency against the current threat landscape. This capability directly addresses the risk of malicious content — ransomware, trojans, weaponized documents — entering Platform Gainwell data platforms through B2B file exchange, internal application uploads, or API-based file submissions.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect (PR.DS — Data Security; PR.PT — Protective Technology) and CSF Detect (DE.CM — Security Continuous Monitoring); addresses the obligation to prevent malicious code from entering systems that store PHI and regulated data, and to detect and notify security operations when malicious content is identified at the ingest boundary.
**Regulatory Relevance**: HIPAA Security Rule §164.308(a)(1) (Security Management Process — threat identification), §164.308(a)(5)(ii)(B) (Protection from Malicious Software); NIST 800-53 SI-3 (Malicious Code Protection), SI-3(2) (Automatic Updates), IR-6 (Incident Reporting), AU-9 (Protection of Audit Information)
**Key Stakeholders**: Platform Engineering, Security Operations Center, Security Architecture, Application and Integration teams operating ingest channels
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-CLOUD-FILE-SCAN-2.6.11](GUID-SEC-CLOUD-FILE-SCAN-2.6.11.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Inbound File Scanning governs antivirus/malware scanning of files at the point of ingest. It does not govern: runtime behavioral detection of executing workloads after a clean file has been promoted (Workload Protection — [GUID-SEC-CLOUD-WORKLOAD-PROT-2.6.04](GUID-SEC-CLOUD-WORKLOAD-PROT-2.6.04.md)); data loss prevention scanning for sensitive data exfiltration (Data Security domain — GUID-SEC-DATA-DLP-2.5.05); scanning of data already at rest in destination stores; or OS/container-level vulnerability scanning (Vulnerability Management — [GUID-SEC-CLOUD-VULN-MGMT-2.6.09](GUID-SEC-CLOUD-VULN-MGMT-2.6.09.md)).
